The first time I saw the ocean, I was six years old. My family had driven to the Outer Banks for a weekend, and I remember standing on the shore, the wind tugging at my hair, the sand warm beneath my feet. The waves crashed in a rhythm that felt like a heartbeat, and for the first time, I understood the vastness of the world. It wasn’t just the endless blue stretching to the horizon—it was the way the water moved, always in motion, always changing, yet somehow the same.

I’ve always been drawn to things that feel infinite. The ocean, the sky, the stars—these are the things that remind me how small I am, and yet, how connected. There’s a strange comfort in that. It’s humbling, but not in a way that makes me feel insignificant. Instead, it makes me feel part of something bigger, something timeless.

I think that’s why I love writing. Words are my way of trying to capture those fleeting moments of beauty or meaning—the way the light hits the water at dawn, the quiet ache of nostalgia when a song comes on the radio, the way a stranger’s smile can change the whole day. Writing is my attempt to hold onto those things, to make them last just a little longer.

Sometimes, I wonder if the ocean ever feels lonely. Does it miss the shore when the tide pulls it back? Does it ever wish it could stay still, just for a moment? I don’t know. But I do know that the ocean, like life, is always moving forward, always changing, always finding its way. And maybe that’s okay. Maybe the beauty is in the journey, not the destination.
